strengths: Ambitious and relevant problem: zero-shot forecasting of chaotic dynamics is important for scientific machine learning, and the paper targets a meaningful gap between generic time-series foundation models and dynamics-aware models.
The proposed synthetic data generation pipeline is interesting: evolutionary recombination plus selection for chaoticity could be a useful resource if released and validated carefully.
The architecture is well motivated by dynamical-systems ideas, especially multichannel attention and patch embeddings inspired by delay/Koopman-style representations.

The synthetic benchmark is large, with evaluation on thousands of held-out generated systems, several metrics, ablations, and comparisons to strong general time-series foundation models including a fine-tuned Chronos baseline.
The scaling-law experiment is a nice and conceptually clean attempt to separate the value of dynamical-system diversity from the value of more trajectories from the same systems.
weaknesses: The main empirical claims are stronger than the evidence. The real-world and PDE evaluations are visually compelling but under-specified: sample sizes, preprocessing, normalization, channel construction, exact train/test protocols, and numeric results are not sufficiently clear from the manuscript.

The zero-shot claim is partly limited by the data generation setup. Held-out synthetic systems appear to be sampled from the same evolutionary procedure and same founder pool as training systems, so it is unclear how much generalization is to genuinely new dynamical families versus interpolation within the generator distribution.

Baselines are incomplete for the scientific-dynamics setting. The paper compares mostly against generic time-series foundation models, but omits or underemphasizes strong dynamics-specific methods such as reservoir computing/NVAR-style models, neural operators or PDE foundation models for the PDE setting, and local adaptation baselines that are common in chaotic forecasting.

The PDE claim is overextended. Forecasting two PDE benchmarks without retraining is interesting, but the setup is not described in enough detail, and two cases do not justify broad statements about spontaneous PDE forecasting ability.

Ablation results are somewhat mixed: the dynamics embedding and MLM pretraining do not consistently improve performance, and the conclusions about which components matter are less clean than the narrative suggests.

Interpretability claims based on attention maps and nonlinear resonance are speculative. The analyses are intriguing, but they do not establish that the observed attention structures causally explain forecasting performance.

Reproducibility is limited. Important implementation details are missing or scattered, including optimizer settings, learning-rate schedule, normalization, exact split construction, seeds, integration settings for all datasets, baseline tuning, and whether code/data will be released.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: figures carry much of the evidence without enough tables or numeric effect sizes, some text has typographical/formatting problems, and some mathematical descriptions of the generated systems and selection filters are not precise enough to independently reproduce.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and relevant problem: out-of-domain forecasting for chaotic dynamical systems using pretraining over many synthetic systems.
The proposed synthetic data generation pipeline is ambitious and, if released and validated, could be a useful resource for studying generalization in nonlinear dynamics.
The architecture choices are motivated by dynamical-systems considerations, especially multichannel attention for coupled variables and patch embeddings related to delay/Koopman-style features.
The paper includes several types of evaluation beyond one benchmark: held-out synthetic systems, a few experimental datasets, scaling with system diversity, ablations, and PDE demonstrations.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are much stronger than the evidence. Most quantitative evaluation is on systems generated by the same evolutionary procedure as training, so the main benchmark does not convincingly establish broad out-of-distribution or universal chaotic-dynamics generalization.

The real-world and PDE experiments are too limited to support claims of emergent zero-shot forecasting of experimental systems or PDEs. They use only a few datasets, unclear preprocessing/normalization choices, short horizons, and limited baselines, with no strong comparison to established dynamical-systems methods such as reservoir computing, neural operators, local/state-space methods, or task-specific trained models.

The baseline suite is not fully appropriate. Comparisons are mainly against general time-series foundation models, many of which are not designed for deterministic multichannel chaotic systems. The paper lacks simpler but critical controls such as PatchTST trained on the same data, equally sized multivariate transformers without the proposed embedding, nearest-neighbor/template baselines over the synthetic system library, and classical chaos forecasting methods.

There are potential leakage and distribution concerns in the synthetic split. Although founder systems are held out, the train/test systems share the same generation mechanism, filtering criteria, augmentations, and numerical integration pipeline. This may reward learning artifacts of the generator rather than general principles of nonlinear dynamics.

The dataset construction is under-validated. The paper relies on several heuristic chaos filters, but does not quantify false positives/false negatives, topological diversity, duplicate/near-duplicate systems, sensitivity to integration tolerances, or whether discovered systems are genuinely novel rather than simple recombinations/rescalings of founders.

Ablations do not cleanly support the architectural story. Some components have mixed effects, MLM can hurt rollout, and the claimed advantage of dynamics embeddings is nuanced, yet the paper presents these choices as broadly validated.

The interpretability section is speculative. Attention-map structures and sinusoidal probing are visually suggestive but do not establish nonlinear resonance or mechanistic understanding; the analysis lacks rigorous controls tying these patterns to forecasting performance.

The scaling-law claim is overstated. The fitted curve is based on a small controlled sweep within one synthetic generator, and the paper does not show robustness across seeds, generator variants, model sizes, or compute/data budgets sufficient to justify calling it a neural scaling law for differential equations.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a top-tier submission. The paper does not clearly provide code, full dataset release details, exact preprocessing for real/PDE benchmarks, baseline tuning protocols, uncertainty across training seeds, or enough implementation detail to verify the large empirical claims.

The writing repeatedly uses broad language such as 'universal', 'spontaneously develops', and 'generalizable properties of dynamics' that is not justified by the current experiments. This overclaiming substantially weakens the paper's scientific credibility.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem: building pretrained models for out-of-domain forecasting of chaotic dynamics is important for SciML and time-series foundation models.

The synthetic data generation pipeline is a meaningful contribution. The evolutionary recombination, chaoticity selection, and large held-out system split provide a richer benchmark than simple parameter perturbations of a few named systems.
Panda's architecture is well motivated by dynamical-systems considerations, especially channel attention for coupled variables and patch embeddings inspired by delay/Koopman-style representations.

The empirical story is broad and promising: strong zero-shot results on held-out synthetic systems, experimental datasets, scaling with number of distinct systems, attention analyses, and preliminary PDE forecasting.
The scaling experiment is particularly interesting because it controls total timepoints while varying dynamical-system diversity, supporting the central thesis that diversity of attractors matters.
The paper is clearly written overall and connects model design choices to relevant nonlinear dynamics theory rather than presenting a generic transformer application.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not fully isolate the contributions of architecture versus synthetic pretraining data. Stronger baselines trained from scratch on the same synthetic data, such as standard PatchTST variants, NVAR/reservoir-style models, neural operators, or other multivariate transformers, would make the claims more convincing.

Comparisons to specialist chaotic forecasting methods are limited. The paper mostly compares against general time-series foundation models, which may understate the difficulty relative to established SciML baselines on chaotic ODE/PDE forecasting.

The PDE result is intriguing but under-specified and somewhat overstated. More detail is needed on how spatial fields are represented as channels, how baselines are configured, what horizons are evaluated, and whether the advantage persists against PDE-specialized or locally trained models.

Some central claims use strong language, such as 'spontaneously develops' PDE forecasting and 'universal' representation, but the evidence remains preliminary and confined to two PDEs plus a few experimental datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: the discovered ODE dataset, evolutionary search details, exact filtering thresholds beyond the appendix, preprocessing/normalization, and train/test generation code would need to be released for the work to be fully verifiable.

The attention/resonance analysis is suggestive but not yet a rigorous mechanistic explanation. Entropy patterns and visual attention maps are interesting, but the link to nonlinear resonance and forecasting ability is not causally established.

Some ablation results complicate the architectural narrative: the dynamics embedding and MLM pretraining do not uniformly help, and the paper could better explain when these components are beneficial versus harmful.

The real-world experimental evaluation is promising but appears limited in scope and sample size; broader datasets, noise/irregular sampling stress tests, and uncertainty estimates would strengthen the practical significance.

strengths: Timely and interesting problem: zero-shot forecasting for chaotic dynamical systems is important for SciML, and the paper tackles it with a clear synthetic-pretraining agenda rather than only per-system fitting.

The proposed data-generation pipeline is creative and fairly well described, combining mutation/recombination of known chaotic ODEs with multiple attractor/chaoticity filters and held-out founder systems to reduce direct train-test overlap.

Panda's architecture incorporates plausible dynamics-aware design choices, especially patching, cross-channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier features motivated by delay embeddings and Koopman-style lifts.

The empirical study is broad relative to many papers in this area: held-out synthetic ODEs, experimental double-pendulum/eigenworm/circuit data, long-horizon distributional metrics, ablations, scaling with system diversity, and initial PDE transfer results.

Results against generic time-series foundation model baselines are consistently favorable, including a fine-tuned Chronos baseline, and the paper reports multiple metrics plus some statistical testing.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are mostly against generic time-series foundation models, not enough against strong dynamics-specific alternatives such as reservoir computing/NGRC, neural ODE/RNN approaches with adaptation, operator-learning/PDE foundation models, or recent OOD dynamical-system reconstruction methods. This makes the practical significance of the gains harder to judge.

The PDE claim is overstated. It is based on only two PDE benchmarks, with VKVS reduced by PCA and no comparison to relevant PDE/operator baselines; calling this an emergent general PDE forecasting capability is stronger than the evidence supports.

The real-world evaluation is visually and empirically promising but narrow, and appears to rely mainly on Chronos-SFT as the comparator. More datasets, uncertainty over preprocessing choices, and stronger baselines are needed before claiming robust real-world transfer.

Long-horizon behavior remains partly unresolved: the authors note Panda can regress to the mean beyond the trained horizon, and MLM pretraining can hurt rollout performance. This weakens claims about learning a general dynamical propagator.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript has a 'Code available:' footnote with no actual link, and the dataset generation/training procedure is computationally heavy enough that missing code/data would materially limit verification.

Some ablations leave ambiguity about which components are truly responsible for performance; the dynamics embedding has mixed effects depending on MLM/rollout setting, and there is limited comparison to simpler multivariate patched transformer variants trained under matched conditions.

The synthetic test distribution is still generated by the same evolutionary recipe as training, albeit from held-out founders. This is reasonable but may overestimate out-of-domain generalization to genuinely different physical systems.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in scientific machine learning: building forecasting models that generalize across nonlinear chaotic dynamical systems rather than fitting one system at a time.

The synthetic data generation pipeline is ambitious and reasonably well motivated, combining curated chaotic ODEs with mutation, skew-product recombination, numerical integration, and several attractor/chaoticity filters.
The model design includes sensible inductive biases for multivariate dynamics, especially patching, channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier feature embeddings inspired by Koopman/DMD-style lifting.

The paper reports broad empirical coverage: held-out synthetic ODEs, several experimental datasets, long-horizon distributional metrics, ablations, patch-size studies, scaling experiments, and two PDE examples.
The appendix contains useful implementation details on integration tolerances, training setup, hardware, and additional metrics, which improves interpretability of the experimental setup.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for the paper's broad claims. Most central results are against generic time-series foundation models such as Chronos, TimesFM, and Time-MoE, rather than strong domain-specific SciML baselines such as reservoir computing, neural ODE/RNN methods for chaos, operator-learning models, local system identification methods, or specialist PDE models.

The main held-out benchmark is still generated by the authors' own evolutionary procedure, with test systems drawn from the same design family as training systems. Holding out founder systems helps, but this is not sufficient evidence for the claimed universal or out-of-domain generalization across nonlinear dynamics.

The real-world evaluation is thin: only a few datasets are considered, comparisons are mainly to Chronos-SFT, and there is little analysis of preprocessing choices, noise, missingness, nonstationarity, or whether stronger per-dataset trained models would outperform the proposed zero-shot model.

The PDE claim is overstated. The paper evaluates only two PDE settings, apparently after dimensionality reduction for VKVS, and does not compare to relevant PDE/operator-learning baselines. Calling this an emergent PDE forecasting capability is stronger than the evidence supports.

Several ablation results complicate the story rather than cleanly supporting it: the dynamics embedding and MLM pretraining have mixed effects, MLM can hurt rollout, and the best patch length varies with horizon. The paper does not fully reconcile these findings with its architectural claims.

The long-term forecasting discussion acknowledges mean regression in Panda rollouts. Distributional metrics may still improve over Chronos, but this does not establish high-quality chaotic forecasting, especially without stronger qualitative and quantitative comparisons to methods designed for attractor preservation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The main text has a placeholder-like 'Code available:' note, and important details such as exact dataset release, filtering thresholds beyond selected tests, baseline tuning, sampling protocols, and full preprocessing pipelines are not clearly sufficient for independent replication.

The scaling-law claim is underdeveloped. The experiment varies number of systems versus initial conditions while holding timepoints fixed, but the observed relationship is empirical and narrow; it is not enough to justify the stronger language around a neural scaling law for differential equations.

Overall, the work is ambitious and potentially useful, but the contribution currently reads as a specialized engineering pipeline with insufficiently rigorous baselines and overextended claims. I would not consider it competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: out-of-domain forecasting for chaotic dynamical systems, where standard time-series models are often poorly matched to the structure of the data.

The synthetic data generation pipeline is a meaningful contribution in its own right. The evolutionary construction of many chaotic skew-product ODEs, together with multiple chaos/stationarity filters and held-out descendant splits, is creative and well motivated.

Panda's architecture is clearly tailored to dynamical systems: patching, channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier lifted embeddings are all connected to relevant theory rather than being arbitrary engineering choices.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing: held-out synthetic chaotic systems, experimental systems, long-horizon distributional metrics, ablations, scaling experiments, and PDE transfer tests all point in a consistent positive direction.

The ablations are useful and honest. They show that channel attention and pretraining choices matter, and the paper reports nontrivial interactions such as MLM improving some settings while hurting rollout performance.
The paper is clearly written, well positioned relative to time-series foundation models and SciML, and includes substantial appendix detail on training, metrics, scaling, and failure modes.
weaknesses: The strongest claims, especially “emergent PDE forecasting capability,” are somewhat overstated. The PDE evaluation is narrow, uses only two systems, and does not compare against strong PDE/operator-learning or reservoir-computing baselines trained or adapted in reasonable ways.

The main comparisons are mostly against generic time-series foundation models. For a SciML audience, additional baselines such as reservoir computers, neural operators, SINDy-style/local learned propagators, or PatchTST/Panda-like architectures trained on comparable synthetic data would better isolate the contribution.

The synthetic held-out evaluation is large but still drawn from the same evolutionary generator and founder family structure. This supports generalization within the proposed synthetic distribution, but only partially supports claims about general chaotic dynamics.

Some methodological choices need clearer justification: training on only 3 randomly sampled channels but evaluating on full multivariate systems, using descendant-based splits, and selecting/normalizing timescales could all introduce favorable inductive biases or hidden distributional alignment.

Long-horizon behavior remains imperfect. The paper acknowledges mean regression in Panda rollouts, so claims about preserving long-term geometry should be framed carefully despite favorable aggregate distributional metrics.

Reproducibility is not fully established in the manuscript: the code footnote appears incomplete, and the dataset generation/training pipeline is complex enough that released code, data, and exact splits are important for validating the results.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: out-of-domain forecasting for chaotic dynamical systems, where standard time-series foundation models are not well aligned with the structure of the data.

The proposed synthetic-data generation pipeline is interesting and potentially useful beyond this paper. The evolutionary skew-product construction, attractor filtering, and diversity analyses provide a plausible route to scaling chaotic ODE data.

The empirical evaluation on held-out generated systems is broad, with thousands of test systems, multiple horizons, several metrics, statistical tests, and comparisons to strong time-series foundation models such as Chronos, TimesFM, TimeMOE, and DynaMix.

The architecture choices are well motivated by dynamical systems considerations, especially patching, channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier feature embeddings. The ablations support the importance of channel attention and show nontrivial interactions among the proposed components.

The paper includes useful appendices with training details, compute requirements, additional metrics, long-horizon distributional analyses, patch-length ablations, scaled-up models, and qualitative examples.
The experimental-data section and PDE transfer experiments make the work more compelling than a purely synthetic benchmark paper, and suggest that the learned model captures useful inductive biases.
weaknesses: The strongest claims are somewhat overstated. In particular, the claim of emergent PDE forecasting is intriguing but not fully established: the PDE evaluation uses only two systems, PCA-reduced or low-resolution representations, and operator-learning baselines that the authors themselves state are not directly comparable because they are trained as one-step predictors and underperform due to setup limitations.

Reproducibility is weaker than expected for a top-tier paper. The extracted reproducibility statement has blank code and checkpoint URLs, so the availability of code, weights, and data is unclear despite the paper relying on a large generated dataset and substantial engineering.

The held-out evaluation is strong in scale but still tests systems produced by the same generation procedure and founder population structure. Holding out 20 founder systems and descendants helps, but the paper does not fully rule out that performance is specialized to the synthetic skew-product distribution rather than broadly to unseen chaotic dynamics.

Some baseline comparisons are caveated or imperfect. DynaMix is included but repeatedly described as not being in its original/fair setting; TimeMOE has NaNs; and larger/fine-tuned Chronos comparisons are constrained by hardware. These issues do not invalidate the results, but they weaken the conclusiveness of the comparisons.

The interpretability section is suggestive but not fully convincing. Attention entropy patterns and qualitative attention maps are used to argue for nonlinear resonance and recurrence-like structure, but the connection to actual forecasting mechanisms is largely correlational.

Long-horizon results are mixed. Panda performs well on some distributional metrics, but alternative KL estimation favors Chronos-SFT/DynaMix, and the paper documents severe mean regression at very long horizons. This tempers the claim that the method preserves long-term chaotic geometry.

The dataset-generation method relies on several heuristic filters and statistical tests for chaoticity/stationarity. While reasonable, false positives/negatives and sensitivity to thresholds are not deeply analyzed, which matters because the training and evaluation distributions are generated by this pipeline.

The real-world experimental evaluation is promising but limited in detail: only a few datasets are used, comparisons appear mainly against Chronos-SFT, and the treatment of noise, missingness, preprocessing, and statistical variability is not described as thoroughly as the synthetic benchmark.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: out-of-domain forecasting for nonlinear/chaotic dynamical systems, where ordinary time-series benchmarks are often a poor proxy for scientific utility.

The synthetic data generation pipeline is ambitious and domain-informed, using evolutionary recombination plus multiple chaos/stationarity filters to build a large collection of candidate chaotic ODEs.

The model design is reasonably motivated: patching, channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier feature embeddings connect naturally to delay embeddings, coupling, and Koopman-style lifted representations.
The held-out synthetic evaluation is large, with thousands of systems and multiple metrics covering both short-term pointwise accuracy and longer-horizon distributional behavior.
The paper includes useful ablations and scaling experiments, and the channel-attention results are a plausible contribution for multivariate dynamical forecasting.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. In particular, the paper repeatedly frames PDE forecasting as an emergent capability, but the PDE experiments are small, use only two systems, rely on PCA-reduced representations, and compare against operator-learning baselines under settings the authors themselves describe as not directly comparable.

Baseline comparisons are uneven. DynaMix is acknowledged as not fairly evaluated, FNO/DeepONet are not matched to the foundation-model setup, and real-world experiments mainly compare against Chronos-SFT rather than a fuller set of strong multivariate or domain-specific baselines.

Several long-horizon conclusions are undermined by the appendix: under the alternative KL implementation and in the tail-only evaluation, Panda is clearly worse than several baselines, suggesting substantial mean regression and weakening claims about preserving invariant geometry.

Reproducibility is a serious concern: the reproducibility statement has blank code/weight links in the extracted manuscript. For a paper centered on a new dataset, pretrained model, and extensive evaluation pipeline, missing accessible artifacts materially lowers confidence.

The dataset novelty and generalization setup need stronger validation. The train/test split holds out founder systems and descendants, but both train and test are generated by the same recombination/search process, so it is unclear how much of the reported zero-shot gain transfers beyond this synthetic distribution.

The real-world experimental section is visually suggestive but thin: it lacks sufficiently detailed quantitative tables, preprocessing details, statistical tests, and comparisons to established system-identification or reservoir-computing methods for these datasets.

Some interpretability claims, such as nonlinear resonance in attention maps and recurrence-like attention structures, are speculative and not tightly connected to forecasting behavior or validated against controlled alternatives.
The paper is broad and polished, but the strongest headline claims depend on the weakest experiments; this makes it below the acceptance threshold despite a technically interesting core contribution.

strengths: Ambitious and timely contribution: the paper tackles out-of-domain forecasting for chaotic dynamics, a meaningful problem for SciML where standard time-series foundation models are not well matched to the structure of the data.

The synthetic dataset construction is a major strength. The evolutionary generation of roughly 20k chaotic ODE systems, coupled with multiple attractor/chaoticity filters and detailed dataset diagnostics, is novel and potentially useful beyond this paper.

The model design is well motivated by dynamical-systems structure: patching, channel attention, polynomial/Fourier lifted embeddings, and fixed-horizon encoder forecasting are all plausible choices, and the paper provides ablations for several of them.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: held-out synthetic systems, real experimental systems, scaling with dynamical diversity, PDE transfer, completion tasks, long-horizon distributional metrics, and interpretability probes.

Results against strong time-series foundation model baselines are convincing on the main zero-shot ODE forecasting task, especially given comparisons to Chronos, TimesFM, TimeMOE, supervised-finetuned Chronos, and DynaMix.
The paper is generally clear, technically detailed, and includes useful appendices with training details, statistical tests, timing comparisons, additional metrics, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The strongest evidence is still concentrated on synthetic systems generated by the authors' own process from a finite founder pool. Although the train/test split is held out, the distributional relationship between discovered systems and the founders makes it hard to know how far the claimed out-of-domain generalization extends.

Some headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially the 'emergent PDE forecasting capability'. The PDE experiments are interesting but limited, and the authors acknowledge that the FNO/DeepONet baselines are not directly comparable and are disadvantaged by the setup.

Long-horizon behavior is mixed. Several appendix metrics show mean regression or cases where Chronos-SFT/DynaMix outperform Panda on very long horizons or alternative KL implementations, which weakens claims about preserving invariant measures over long rollouts.

The real-world experimental evaluation is promising but relatively thin: it appears to focus mainly on comparison to Chronos-SFT, with limited details on dataset splits, statistical uncertainty, and whether stronger domain-specific or recurrent baselines would change the picture.

The ablation story is somewhat complicated: MLM and the dynamics embedding do not consistently improve all settings, and the final architectural choices are justified empirically but not always cleanly separated from training/data effects.

Reproducibility would depend heavily on releasing the generated systems, filtering code, training code, and checkpoints; the manuscript gives many details but does not make the availability of these artifacts fully clear.
